title: The teachers we already have
author: Mark Solomons
summary: Mark Solomons, an economics teacher now in Queensland, reflects on his own 2005 teacher training, which never explained working memory, retrieval practice or the novice-expert distinction and instead pushed maximum engagement and a guide-on-the-side role. Prompted by a former student who has become a teacher in England, he compares that with today's Early Career Framework in England and Australia's Strong Beginnings report, which now require core learning-science content in initial teacher education. His argument is that improving training is not enough, because most teachers are already in schools, new graduates quickly absorb how things are done around here, and ideas can suffer lethal mutations when translated into practice. He draws on Dylan Wiliam's love the one you're with strategy, Rob Coe's view of expertise as knowledge, skills and judgement, and Coe and Kime's call for a revolution in professional learning. He closes by urging schools to measure whether professional learning changed classrooms rather than counting attendance, and to give teachers in their first year or their thirtieth the same access to knowledge.
points: Solomons recalls training that stressed engagement and activities while saying nothing about working memory, retrieval practice or worked examples.
England and Australia now mandate core learning-science content in initial teacher education, but reform of training alone will take years to reach most teachers.
Roughly 78 percent of teachers are beyond their first five years, so investing in the teachers already in schools is essential and influences newcomers.
Good ideas can become lethal mutations, such as retrieval practice shrinking to five questions at the start of every lesson, when the underlying reason is lost.
Professional learning should be judged by whether classroom practice and student results changed, not by attendance or enjoyment.
quotes: What it did focus heavily on was maximum engagement, differentiating lessons for almost everyone and being a ‘guide on the side’, getting out of the students’ way so they could take charge of their own learning.
Back then, observations were focused on demonstrating progress within a lesson…we were judged on student performance, which we know now to be a poor proxy for learning.
Teachers need to know why they are doing something, what the research says and whether it makes sense with those students, in that subject, at that point in the lesson sequence.
If we rely on ITE reform to do all the work, we'll be waiting a long time before most teachers have been through the new training.
So we can’t just expect new teachers to rock up with their new learning into schools and hope the existing teachers pick it all up through osmosis.
Berliner argued that experience alone won’t necessarily make someone an expert, and that the conditions teachers work in have a powerful influence on how their expertise develops.
Queensland is a good example of the difference between doing professional development and developing professionally.
Hearing about something once in a Thursday afternoon session is not going to do much.
Did anything change in classrooms, are teachers still doing it long after the session and did students get anything better as a result?
